newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: INTERVIEW-MAS hopes ticketless plan flies.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-MAS hopes ticketless plan flies.

text.p: Malaysia Airlines (MAS) hopes a newly-introduced "ticketless" system will help it cut processing costs for the nine million passengers who fly on its domestic routes, an executive at the airline said on Tuesday.
About 60 percent or around nine million of MAS's passengers are domestic travellers, said Shamin Ahmad, senior vice president of sales and services.
If all MAS's domestic passengers started using the system, in the long-run, "savings in terms of costs would be substantial", Shamin said in an interview.

The ticketless system has been available since April, but was formally launched on June 10. It allows customers of Malaysia's largest bank, Malayan Banking Bhd (Maybank), to pay for phone-ordered tickets on domestic routes through Maybank's automated teller machines (ATM).
The customer first reserves the tickets through MAS's 24-hour reservation line and gets a transaction number which is keyed in at any of Maybank's and Maybank Finance's 650 ATMs in Malaysia.

Payment can be made by debiting the customer's bank account or through credit cards issued by Maybank. The ATM prints travel details on a slip, which is used at the airport check-in counter to obtain a boarding pass.
MAS may be the first airline in the world to implement such a system, Shamin said.
Maybank has over three million ATM cardholders.

Shamin could not quantify the amount of savings expected from the new system, but said the company could save on staff costs such as cutting back on keypunch operators who manually enter the payment details.
MAS, the nation's flagship carrier, will also be able to book revenues much faster, he said. "It's quick and timely information in terms of revenue accounting."
On the customer side, the system allows for tickets to be paid for at locations other than MAS offices and during off-hours. "ATM machines are practically everywhere," he said.
MAS is looking to add other banks to the system, which was developed in a year by in-house technicians, Shamin said.

Because Maybank is part of the Malaysian Electronic Payment System (MEPS) consortium, which links the ATMs of most of Malaysia's major banks, MAS could extend ticketless purchases to other institutions, Shamin said.
He said MAS's investment in the ticketless project may have run into the hundreds of thousands of ringgit.
The system may also be extended to international routes, Shamin said. However, he noted that such a step must be approved by the International Air Transport Association.
Other technology-related services MAS was looking at included booking tickets through the Internet and setting up self-service ticketing booths, he said.
But such new products were not always welcomed with open arms, Shamin said. Travel agents were concerned ticketless travel would harm their business.
